newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: KL interbank rates rise on finance firms demand.
newsitem.headline: KL interbank rates rise on finance firms demand.

text.p: Interbank rates rose across the board on demand from finance companies and lingering fears of a long-term government bond issue, dealers said on Monday.
One-week money was up at 6.70/80 percent against 6.50 on Friday, but two-week was unchanged at 6.70/80 percent.
One-month money was at 7.40 percent against 7.30/35, three-month at 7.50/55 against 7.40/45 and six-month at 7.55/60 against 7.45/50.
"Finance companies are short again. They are pushing up rates," said a dealer with a Malaysian bank.
"But, the big banks are up there lending. One of the big banks has set the cap on one-month at 7.40," he said.
Dealers said the market was relatively liquid, but rumours of a new bond issue was preventing any fall in rates.
"There's a strong rumour of a new bond issue. This is highly possible given the flush market situation now," said a dealer with a Malaysian bank.

Rumours of a new bond issue first surfaced a few months ago following maturity of a series of bond issues which were not rolled over. Bank Negara last issued long-term government bonds in November 1996.
Interest rate futures on the Malaysia Monetary Exchange were down across the board.
At 0400 GMT, the three-month Kuala Lumpur Interbank Offered Rate (KLIBOR) September contract was down two points to 92.62, or an implied yield of 7.38 percent.
The December contract fell one to 92.74, or 7.26 percent while March 1998 was down three to 92.75, or 7.25 percent.
